C001.name: Extended reality
C001.definition: Extended reality (XR) refers to extending reality by some means. Systematically, it involves using systems to either augment our reality or replace our perception of reality.

C002.name: Virtual reality
C002.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is a specific type of immersive experience mentioned in the course title. It involves creating a simulated environment that users can interact with.

C003.name: Augmented reality
C003.definition: Augmented reality (AR) is another specific type of immersive experience mentioned in the course title. It involves overlaying digital information onto the real world.

C004.name: Mixed reality
C004.definition: Mixed reality (MR) is a distinct term that is currently being heard in the field. It represents a specific type of reality blending.

C005.name: Immersive technology
C005.definition: Immersive technology is a type of technology where the user experiences an environment through sensory organs in such a way that they fail to distinguish it from the real environment. This perceived experience leads the user to assume the environment is real.

C006.name: Reality-virtuality continuum
C006.definition: Reality-virtuality continuum is a scale used to visualize the spectrum between a completely real environment and a completely virtual environment.

C007.name: Virtual environment
C007.definition: Virtual environment is one extreme of the scale where there is nothing real present, meaning the environment is completely virtual.

C008.name: Augmented virtuality
C008.definition: Augmented virtuality is the opposite of augmented reality, where a virtual world is enhanced by incorporating real-world content.

C009.name: Metaverse
C009.definition: The Metaverse is not merely an application of virtual reality, mixed reality, or augmented reality technology. The Metaverse is a broad concept that involves reimagining how humans interact with the digital world in an all-around 3D environment.

C010.name: Human-computer interaction
C010.definition: Human-computer interaction is a different way of looking at how humans interact with digital content. This interaction occurs within a 3D environment using a natural way of interaction.

C011.name: Cognitive side
C011.definition: Cognitive side refers to the understanding of the human mind that is necessary to grasp how our senses influence the desired experience when using technology or a system.

C012.name: Psychological side
C012.definition: Psychological side refers to the understanding of the human mind that is necessary to grasp how our senses influence the desired experience when using technology or a system.

C013.name: Interactions
C013.definition: Interactions refers to the process of designing and implementing how users engage with the environment within VR or AR systems.

C014.name: Virtual tours
C014.definition: Virtual tours are experiences that allow a user to visit a place remotely, even if they cannot physically go there. This method saves both money and physical effort for the user.

C015.name: Heritage tourism
C015.definition: Heritage tourism involves allowing users to explore a heritage place virtually, even if physical visits are restricted. This enables users to explore every part of the heritage space without having to travel there.

C016.name: Preservation of digital heritage
C016.definition: Preservation of digital heritage is the process of digitally saving a heritage space, often in the form of virtual tours. This digital preservation can increase the lifespan and potential for the space to be visited by many users.

C017.name: Non-immersive
C017.definition: Non-immersive refers to a virtual experience obtained through a computer where the user controls activities within the software, but the environment does not directly interact with the user. This type of system relies on psychological engagement, allowing the user to remain physically attached to, a

C018.name: Augmentation
C018.definition: Augmentation is the process of enhancing the real world by overlaying digital content onto it. This focus is distinct from Virtual Reality, which emphasizes a fully simulated environment.

C019.name: Immersive experience
C019.definition: Immersive experience is a concept emphasized in Virtual Reality (VR) where the user is fully enveloped in a simulated environment. This level of immersion is not a mandatory requirement for Augmented Reality (AR).

C020.name: Telemedicine
C020.definition: Telemedicine is an application that enables medical professionals to interact with patients remotely. It is one of the many interesting applications developed using Augmented Reality.

C021.name: Virtual tape measure
C021.definition: Virtual tape measure is an augmented reality application that allows users to measure heights or lengths of objects. This tool eliminates the need for carrying a physical tape measure.

C022.name: Markerless AR application
C022.definition: Markerless AR application is a versatile type of AR that does not require placing any markers in the physical world. These applications function based on computer vision techniques, allowing users to decide where virtual objects are placed.

C023.name: Holographic projection
C023.definition: Holographic projection is an example of a projection-based technique. This technique can be utilized in the development of Augmented Reality (AR) applications.

C024.name: Marker-based
C024.definition: Marker-based systems are easier to create and rely on simple algorithms. However, these systems require a very sanitized environment to maintain the markers, as they are prone to damage in outdoor settings.

C025.name: Markerless
C025.definition: Markerless techniques are used to overcome the maintenance difficulties of markers. These techniques primarily rely on computer vision and may utilize other sensors, such as GPS sensors, for location-based applications.

C026.name: Fully immersive
C026.definition: Fully immersive is one of the three categories of Virtual Reality (VR) systems. This category is defined by the importance of the psychological aspect and the overall experience provided to the user.

C027.name: Superimposition-based
C027.definition: Superimposition-based is a type of computer vision-based application. This application involves placing digital content over the real-world view.

C028.name: Artificial environment
C028.definition: Artificial environment is a computer-generated setting that is not real, which must be populated with artificial objects. This environment can be a graphical representation of either a real world or an imaginary world.

C029.name: Sensory stimuli
C029.definition: Sensory stimuli are computer-generated inputs that a VR system provides to the user. These stimuli allow the user to experience the artificial or synthetic environment through their sensory organs, such as their eyes and ears.

C030.name: Interactivity
C030.definition: Interactivity is the characteristic of a VR system where dynamic changes in the virtual environment occur based on the user's actions or inputs. This allows the user to interact with the elements present in the environment, similar to how they interact with objects in the real world.

C031.name: Non-immersive VR
C031.definition: Non-immersive VR is a screen-based experience that does not meet the criteria for a fully immersive experience. This type of experience is sometimes called regular computer screen based experience.

C032.name: Superimposition
C032.definition: Superimposition is a category of AR system where extra information is placed over the building space. This allows digital content to appear on the real-world view.

C033.name: Phases
C033.definition: Phases are distinct periods into which the evolution of the field can be divided, although some overlap may occur between them.

C034.name: Stereoscopic device
C034.definition: Stereoscopic device is a type of apparatus that allows the brain to interpret two-dimensional images as three-dimensional objects. This device established the possibility of creating a sense of depth from flat images.

C035.name: Stereoscopic vision
C035.definition: Stereoscopic vision is the biological ability of the brain to perceive three-dimensional space by viewing two-dimensional images. This perception allows us to see images together as objects existing in 3D space.

C036.name: Flight simulator
C036.definition: Flight simulator is an early concept developed to provide an immersive experience. It utilizes multiple sensors to simulate the environment, serving as a precursor to modern multi-sensory VR experiences.

C037.name: Head-mounted display
C037.definition: Head-mounted display is a new kind of computer display that people began working on in the 1950s. It is a device worn by the user to display visual information.

C038.name: Haptic feedback
C038.definition: Haptic feedback is a method where touch sensations are provided to the user. This allows the user to feel objects on the screen while manipulating them.

C039.name: CAVE system
C039.definition: CAVE system is a type of immersive environment that used a single computer to render images in a surrounding setting, giving the user the sensation of being surrounded by holograms.

C040.name: WTK package
C040.definition: WTK package is a software package developed in 1992 that provided higher-level tools for application development within Virtual Reality (VR).

C041.name: Virtual Reality Modeling Language
C041.definition: VRML is a modeling language for virtual reality that was presented in 1994, which subsequently led to the appearance of many other modeling languages.

C042.name: Field of view
C042.definition: Field of view is a technical specification, such as the 150-degree FOV, that describes the angular extent of the visual area presented by a Head-Mounted Display (HMD).

C043.name: Growth phase
C043.definition: Growth phase is the last and continuing phase of VR evolution, which began around 2016. This phase is characterized by continuous development and acceleration of the field.

C044.name: Developmental phase
C044.definition: Developmental phase is one of the four evolutionary stages used to describe the history of VR. These phases track the evolution of the technology over time.

C045.name: Experimental phase
C045.definition: Experimental phase is the initial period of development that occurred before the 1980s. This phase was primarily related to early experimentation, which defined concepts and showed the types of technology required.

C046.name: Tools or applications phase
C046.definition: Tools or applications phase is the period spanning from the mid-1990s to 2007. During this phase, early applications and exploratory tasks were developed, focusing on interaction techniques, usability, and design theory related to AR.

C047.name: Commercial application phase
C047.definition: Commercial application phase is the current phase, starting from 2007. This phase is characterized by widespread AR availability and the continuous emergence of newer applications in various market domains.

C048.name: Tracking
C048.definition: Tracking is the process used to register content in 3D, which allows people to see and interact with shared augmented reality content. This technology is specifically done to register the content in three dimensions.

C049.name: Head mounted display
C049.definition: Head mounted display is an optical see-through device that is worn by the user. This device is used to display augmented or virtual content onto the user's view.

C050.name: Computer-generated imagery
C050.definition: Computer-generated imagery is graphics created by a computer that can appear either superimposed over the real world view or as a substitute for the real world view. This imagery is used to augment or replace the user's perception.

C051.name: Prototype AR system
C051.definition: Prototype AR system is an early functional system that combined an optical see-through head mounted display with a ceiling-mounted mechanical tracking system and custom graphics hardware. This system was designed to register 3D content based on head movements.

C052.name: Registration tracking techniques
C052.definition: Registration tracking techniques were research areas carried out during the early development of the field. These techniques helped in the overall development of the field.

C053.name: See-through head mounted displays
C053.definition: See-through head mounted displays were utilized in early research on AR during the period of 1995 and 1996. These displays allowed for the development of AR applications.

C054.name: AR interaction methods
C054.definition: AR interaction methods refer to the ways in which a user can interact with the augmented digital content. Work was carried out on these methods in 1993.

C055.name: Mobile AR systems
C055.definition: Mobile AR systems were a topic of research carried out during the basic research phase. These systems were developed alongside other AR research activities.

C056.name: Viewpoint tracking
C056.definition: Viewpoint tracking is the activity of determining how to track the user's viewpoint. This is necessary so that the registration of content in 3D happens accurately.

C057.name: Wearable computing
C057.definition: Wearable computing refers to devices, such as headsets, where the computer hardware is carried externally, for example in a backpack. Interaction with these devices is achieved through different input devices.

C058.name: AR overlay on real-world marker
C058.definition: AR overlay on real-world marker is a technique that uses computer vision to place augmented reality content onto physical markers in the real world.

C059.name: Commercial phase
C059.definition: Commercial phase is the stage of AR evolution where AR experiences transition from niche research to becoming widely popular and available to the general public. This phase is characterized by increased commercial interest and the potential for AR applications to drive sales and popularity of goods.

C060.name: AR authoring tools
C060.definition: AR authoring tools are software that enable the creation of Augmented Reality experiences. These tools, such as those based on Adobe Flash, made it possible to experience AR directly through web browsers, thus expanding accessibility.

C061.name: ARKit SDK
C061.definition: ARKit SDK is a Software Development Kit launched by Apple for the purpose of developing Augmented Reality systems. This launch significantly stimulated growth in the field by allowing a large number of developers to create AR applications.

C062.name: Tracking and registration in 3D
C062.definition: Tracking and registration in 3D is the process of accurately locating and mapping objects within a three-dimensional space. This capability is expected to become increasingly feasible on low-end devices due to advancements in AI and computer vision.

C063.name: Defining characteristic
C063.definition: Defining characteristics are features that help distinguish between different types of systems. These characteristics allow one to differentiate between a virtual reality system and an augmented reality system, for example.

C064.name: Virtual reality system
C064.definition: Virtual reality system is an artificial environment that is experienced through sensory stimuli. This environment is provided by a computer and allows the user's actions to partially determine what happens within it.

C065.name: Technological issue
C065.definition: Technological issue refers to the challenge of generating suitable stimuli for a virtual environment. This involves figuring out how to create the necessary inputs for the user to experience the virtual world.

C066.name: Psychological issue
C066.definition: Psychological issue refers to the challenge of how a user perceives the stimuli that have been generated. This relates to the human factor and how individual psychological characteristics affect perception.

C067.name: Sensory organs
C067.definition: Sensory organs are the biological mechanisms that are activated in a suitable way to receive input. Activation of one or more sensory organs is what technology can do to generate an immersive experience.

C068.name: Immersion
C068.definition: Immersion is the objective or technological experience provided by a system. Immersion aids the potential for a user to feel present in a virtual world.

C069.name: Extensive
C069.definition: Extensive refers to the range of sensory modalities that are presented to the user. The more sensory organs that are stimulated by the stimuli provided by the computer, the more extensive the immersion is.

C070.name: Matching
C070.definition: Matching refers to the congruence between different sensory modalities. For instance, the visual presentation must instantly correspond to head motion and the virtual representation of the user's body.

C071.name: Surrounding
C071.definition: Surrounding is the extent to which the cues provided are panoramic. This refers to the scope of the field of view for visual senses or the extent of auditory perception for sound sources.

C072.name: Vivid
C072.definition: Vivid is the quality of energy stimulated within a particular sensory modality. This quality relates to how much energy the computer generates to stimulate a sensory organ, which is enhanced by factors such as resolution, lighting, and audio bitrate.

C073.name: Presence
C073.definition: Presence is the subjective experience of feeling truly located within a virtual world. Presence is achieved when a user is unable to distinguish between the real world and the virtual world.

C074.name: Representational fidelity
C074.definition: Representational fidelity is the degree to which the VR experience conveys a place that is or could be on Earth. This fidelity measures how closely the VR experience matches or exploits the familiarity of a real-world place.

C075.name: Experiential fidelity
C075.definition: Experiential fidelity is the degree to which the user's personal experience matches the intended experience of the VR creator. Higher experiential fidelity is achieved when real-world constraints are incorporated into the virtual world's navigation, movement, and interaction.

C076.name: Immersion
C076.definition: Immersion is a concept tied to the technological issues of Virtual Reality (VR) systems. It relates to the technological aspects of the VR experience.

C077.name: Pose
C077.definition: Pose refers to the viewer's position and orientation within the context of the system. Pose determination is necessary to register virtual content in the real world.

C078.name: Registration phase
C078.definition: Registration phase determines the pose of a viewer relative to a real world anchor. This phase is performed when the user begins using the system.

C079.name: Tracking phase
C079.definition: Tracking phase is the process that follows registration, requiring the continuous updating of the viewer's pose relative to a previously known pose. This is necessary because the user is likely to move while using the AR application.

C080.name: Real world anchor
C080.definition: Real world anchor is a physical element in the environment used by the system to anchor virtual content. This allows the virtual content to appear as a seamless part of the physical environment.

C081.name: Uncanny valley effect
C081.definition: The uncanny valley effect is a phenomenon where making environments familiar to the user can sometimes lead to feelings of uneasiness or creepiness. This occurs even when the objective is to make the environment as familiar as possible to the user's real-world experience.

C082.name: Cyber sickness
C082.definition: Cyber sickness is a major concern related to VR systems that will be discussed in detail. The discussion will cover its causes, how it can be measured, and strategies to reduce or eliminate it.

C083.name: Mitigation
C083.definition: Mitigation refers to the strategies that can be adopted to overcome the challenges associated with cybersickness. Finding a feasible solution to reduce the impact of cybersickness is extremely important in the context of VR systems.

C084.name: Evaluation
C084.definition: Evaluation refers to the process of measuring or assessing cybersickness. This process helps determine how to know if cybersickness has happened or is going to happen.

C085.name: Causes
C085.definition: Causes refers to the factors that can lead to cybersickness. It is important to understand that not a single factor is responsible for this condition.

C086.name: Motion sickness susceptibility
C086.definition: Motion sickness susceptibility is an internal factor referring to an individual's tendency to experience motion sickness. This susceptibility is related to Cyber sickness because both conditions involve the brain receiving conflicting sensory signals.

C087.name: Body awareness
C087.definition: Body awareness is the ability of the user to attend to and perceive bodily sensations. This awareness can be affected by factors such as poor sleep quality.

C088.name: Inter-pupillary distance
C088.definition: Inter-pupillary distance (IPD) is the distance between the user's pupils. This distance determines how stereoscopic vision is achieved through the HMDs.

C089.name: Display resolution
C089.definition: Display resolution is a hardware factor that determines the clarity of the visual experience. Higher resolution generally leads to a better experience and reduced cybersickness up to a specific point.

C090.name: Latency
C090.definition: Latency is the time gap between an action performed in the physical world and the corresponding change reflected in the virtual world. Increased latency is found to increase the likelihood of inducing sickness.

C091.name: Latency jitter
C091.definition: Latency jitter is the variability in the time gap between a user's action and its reflection in the virtual world. This variability causes irregularities in the timing of data delivery, leading to discomfort and disorientation.

C092.name: Type of display
C092.definition: Type of display is a hardware factor that significantly influences the severity of cybersickness symptoms. Users utilizing Head-Mounted Displays (HMDs) tend to feel more cyber sick compared to those using conventional monitors.

C093.name: Type of input
C093.definition: Type of input refers to the various methods used in virtual reality, such as hand controllers or treadmills. The specific input device or technology used can cause cybersickness to vary.

C094.name: Visual motion
C094.definition: Visual motion stimulus is the movement experienced by the user within a virtual environment. This stimulus is considered one of the primary causes of cyber sickness, and its severity is affected by how the content moves.

C095.name: Vection
C095.definition: Vection is the sensation of self-motion, which is the feeling of movement experienced by the user. This sensation is highest when the user perceives motion in peripheral stimuli.

C096.name: Means of locomotion
C096.definition: Means of locomotion refers to how a user is moving within the virtual world. This aspect of movement affects cyber sickness because a mismatch between virtual and physical movements can cause disorientation.

C097.name: Questionnaire-based input
C097.definition: Questionnaire-based input is a method of input where users rate their discomfort or disorientation using self-report scales. These scales are typically administered before, during, or after the experience.

C098.name: Physiological input
C098.definition: Physiological input is an objective method used to detect cybersickness by measuring bodily functions. Examples of these inputs include heart rate, galvanic skin response, and EEG.

C099.name: Behavioral input
C099.definition: Behavioral input involves detecting cybersickness using observable cues related to how a user moves. These cues include head and body movement, blink rate, and postural sway.

C100.name: Content-based input
C100.definition: Content-based input measures cybersickness by analyzing features within the virtual reality environment itself. These features include optical flow and depth cues.

C101.name: Simulator Sickness Questionnaire
C101.definition: Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) is a widely used questionnaire designed to measure cybersickness. It contains 16 items divided into subscales for oculomotor, disorientation, and nausea symptoms.

C102.name: Manual evaluation
C102.definition: Manual evaluation is a measurement technique that relies on human intervention to assess cyber sickness. This process requires someone to distribute questionnaires, collect feedback, and analyze responses to determine the severity or onset of cyber sickness.

C103.name: Automated evaluation
C103.definition: Automated evaluation is a measurement technique that uses automated algorithms to measure cyber sickness. This method processes various inputs, such as physiological or biometric data, to automatically determine the presence of cyber sickness.

C104.name: Transparent models
C104.definition: Transparent models are types of models that provide clear insight into their internal workings and decision-making process. When an automated evaluation uses these models, the process is easily understood.

C105.name: Stepwise regression analysis
C105.definition: Stepwise regression analysis is a method utilized to measure cyber sickness using a variety of physiological signals. This technique is considered to be a transparent model.

C106.name: Cybersickness
C106.definition: Cybersickness is the specific topic currently being discussed in the course, which is the focus of this lecture segment.

C107.name: Questionnaire-based subjective input
C107.definition: Questionnaire-based subjective input is a type of input collected by using questionnaires to gather subjective data.

C108.name: Physiological and biometric input
C108.definition: Physiological and biometric input is a type of input that involves collecting data related to the body's functions and biological measurements.

C109.name: Interpretable black box model
C109.definition: Interpretable black box model is one of the models being discussed for evaluation, which is contrasted with other evaluation models.

C110.name: Mitigation strategies
C110.definition: Mitigation strategies are methods, implemented by either the developer or the user, designed to reduce the negative effects of cybersickness. These strategies aim to lessen the severity of the symptoms.

C111.name: Interpretable model
C111.definition: Interpretable models are similar to transparent models and offer flexibility in how they are used. Interpretable models provide precise details regarding the relationship between the input provided and the output received.

C112.name: Black box model
C112.definition: Black box models are types of models whose decision-making process is shrouded in mystery and cannot be easily understood. The model simply takes input and produces an output, making the relationship between them difficult to discern.

C113.name: Hybrid model
C113.definition: Hybrid models are combinations of different Machine Learning models designed to achieve both high accuracy and transparency in their decision-making process. Combining multiple ML models results in a hybrid model.

C114.name: Prediction
C114.definition: Prediction is the ability to anticipate upcoming Cybersickness (CS) incidents before they happen, allowing for potential mitigation measures.

C115.name: Detection
C115.definition: Detection is the process of identifying Cybersickness (CS) after the experience has already taken place, meaning the input is generated after the experience.

C116.name: Classification labels
C116.definition: Classification labels are an output from machine learning-based evaluation that indicates the likelihood or severity of Cybersickness (CS).

C117.name: Sickness score
C117.definition: Sickness score is a numerical value that quantifies the severity of the Cybersickness (CS) experience.

C118.name: Self-report questionnaire
C118.definition: Self-report questionnaire is a tool used to gather data for Cybersickness (CS) evaluation, providing users with rating scales to provide scores.

C119.name: User experience
C119.definition: User experience is the overall experience that is impacted if the user's presence is affected. Developers aim to develop strategies without compromising this experience.

C120.name: Developer's perspective
C120.definition: The developer's perspective is the way developers view the problem and how they can address it. This involves determining what the developers can do to solve the issue.

C121.name: User's perspective
C121.definition: The user's perspective involves what users can do to prevent cyber sickness. This highlights that proper usage is necessary even if a good solution is provided.

C122.name: Symmetric mask
C122.definition: Symmetric mask is a classical approach that occludes the periphery in reaction to translational and/or angular velocity.

C123.name: Ground visible restrictor
C123.definition: Ground visible restrictor is a technique that ensures the ground plane remains visible during movement.

C124.name: Dynamic visual blur
C124.definition: Dynamic visual blur is a technique that reduces the possibility of cyber sickness by obscuring or reducing the clarity of the visual environment. This technique can be implemented using two types of blur effects.

C125.name: Depth of field blur
C125.definition: Depth of field blur is a type of visual blur effect that utilizes well-known depth cues found in human vision. This effect is one of the two types of dynamic visual blur.

C126.name: Peripheral blur
C126.definition: Peripheral blur is a type of visual blur effect that specifically targets the peripheral areas of the user's vision. This effect is one of the two types of dynamic visual blur.

C127.name: Rest frame
C127.definition: Rest frame is a fixed element within the virtual environment that remains stationary relative to the real world, regardless of the user's movements. These frames are used as a technique to reduce cyber sickness.

C128.name: Optical flow manipulation
C128.definition: Optical flow manipulation is a technique that involves visually mixing optical flow patterns in the reverse direction of the virtual visual motion. This manipulation aims to reduce the perceived optical flow.

C129.name: Sparse peripheral display
C129.definition: Sparse peripheral display is a hardware addition that expands the periphery of a Head-Mounted Display (HMD) using a colorful LED matrix. This modification is used to reduce the effects of cybersickness.

C130.name: Phantom legs
C130.definition: Phantom legs is a technique that uses additional hardware to apply alternating haptic cues synchronized with the user's footsteps. This method was found to manage to reduce cybersickness to a great extent.

C131.name: Floor vibrations
C131.definition: Floor vibrations is a technique that utilizes vibration-driven whole body tactile feedback. It attempts to match the vibrations that occur in the virtual environment.

C132.name: Modified motion platform
C132.definition: Modified motion platform is a piece of hardware that can be adjusted to reduce cybersickness. Short bursts of rotational acceleration can be used to match the visual forward acceleration to achieve this effect.

C133.name: Viewpoint snapping
C133.definition: Viewpoint snapping is a modification to locomotion technique that renders moving pictures in discrete chunks during rotation. This technique is used to reduce the exposure or duration of virtual exposure.

C134.name: Habituation
C134.definition: Habituation is a process where the intensity of cyber sickness gradually decreases after a person experiences the virtual environment repeatedly. This gradual reduction in symptoms is achieved through repeated exposure.

C135.name: Internal
C135.definition: Internal causes are subjective factors that relate to a user's personal characteristics, such as age or gender. These factors are inherent to the individual experiencing the symptoms.

C136.name: External
C136.definition: External causes are related to the physical components or the content being presented. These issues can stem from either the hardware or the content itself.

C137.name: Evaluation strategies
C137.definition: Evaluation strategies are methods used to measure cybersickness, involving inputs, a process (which can be manual or automated), and outputs like classes or numerical values. These strategies help quantify the severity of the sickness.

C138.name: VR hardware
C138.definition: VR hardware refers to the physical components, such as computers, headsets, and controllers, that are used to create the VR experience. These components are part of the overall VR setup.

C139.name: Stimulation
C139.definition: Stimulation is the stimuli that the hardware produces, which overrides the senses of the user. This process is referred to as the stimulation data flow.

C140.name: Surrounding physical world
C140.definition: The surrounding physical world is the real-world environment that must be considered part of the VR system. This is necessary because the user may respond to stimuli, such as light or sound, coming from this real environment.

C141.name: Head tracking
C141.definition: Head tracking is the most critical type of tracking commonly utilized in Virtual Reality (VR). It monitors the movement of the user's head.

C142.name: Display or output device
C142.definition: Display or output device is any device that produces output to stimulate a user's sensory organs. This term is used broadly and does not require the device to be a visual display.

C143.name: Sensor or input device
C143.definition: Sensor or input device refers to any tracking device that captures user input. Sensors are devices that extract information from the real world, specifically tracking user movements.

C144.name: Computer or processing part
C144.definition: Computer or processing part is a device that processes inputs and produces outputs. This element allows the user to perceive the virtual world.

C145.name: World grounded devices
C145.definition: World grounded devices are input devices that are fixed in the real world and do not move. These devices are often used to interact with grounded desktop or systems.

C146.name: Non-tracked handheld controllers
C146.definition: Non-tracked handheld controllers are devices held in the hand but are not tracked in 3D space by the system. Because they are not tracked, the system does not know the controller's exact position relative to a reference frame.

C147.name: Bend sensing gloves
C147.definition: Bend sensing gloves are a type of data glove that detects hand postures and gestures because sensors are placed at all bend positions or joints. The processing unit receives continuous raw data from these sensors to detect the gesture.

C148.name: Bare hand inputs
C148.definition: Bare hand inputs are interactions where the system tracks the bare hand using computer vision techniques. This allows users to provide gestures without needing to wear or use any external device.

C149.name: Non-hand-based input device
C149.definition: Non-hand-based input device captures input from parts of the body other than the hand, such as head movement, eye gaze, or voice. These devices allow the system to capture input from various parts of the user's body.

C150.name: Head tracking based input device
C150.definition: Head tracking based input device uses the user's head motion for input, detecting movement along axes like yaw, roll, and pitch. This detection allows the device to infer the kind of input and change the view accordingly.

C151.name: Eye tracker
C151.definition: Eye tracker is a device, often integrated with headsets, that tracks how the user's eyes are moving. The system uses this movement to infer the user's intent and take necessary action.

C152.name: Midas touch problem
C152.definition: Midas touch problem is a difficulty in eye tracking where the system cannot differentiate whether a user's gaze is intentional for selection or merely a natural, purposeless blank gaze. This inability can cause the system to select objects when the user did not intend to.

C153.name: Multimodal input
C153.definition: Multimodal input is a preferred method of interaction that utilizes multiple forms of input. This approach works better than relying solely on eye tracking-based input.

C154.name: Full-body tracking
C154.definition: Full-body tracking is a non-hand input method that tracks movement of more than just the head and hands. This tracking adds to the illusion of self-embodiment and social presence in the virtual world because the user sees a fuller representation of themselves.

C155.name: Motion capture suit
C155.definition: Motion capture suit (MOCAP) is an approach to full-body tracking that utilizes a suit containing various sensors. These sensors capture and transmit raw movement data from different parts of the body, which is then converted into full body position and movement.

C156.name: Camera-based tracking
C156.definition: Camera-based tracking is an input method that uses multiple surrounding cameras to detect movement. The system infers the overall body movement of a character by detecting the movement of fiducial markers worn by the actor.

C157.name: Sound tracking
C157.definition: Sound tracking is a non-hand input technique that captures voice, speech, and non-speech sound. This input is captured using devices like microphones or microphone arrays for interaction within the virtual world.

C158.name: Inertial measurement unit
C158.definition: Inertial measurement unit (IMU) is a type of sensor contained within motion capture suits. These sensors capture and transmit raw movement data when body movement happens, which is then combined and converted to full body position and movement.

C159.name: Computer
C159.definition: Computer is a device that processes data coming from input sensors and then activates or actuates the output devices. This processing is central to the function of the VR system.

C160.name: Graphics Processing Unit
C160.definition: Graphics Processing Unit is a specialized processor typically used to speed up the rendering process. This speed is achieved because of its inherent ability to perform parallel processing.

C161.name: Middleware
C161.definition: Middleware is a type of software that is required to support and render, and to develop, virtual reality experiences. It acts as a necessary layer for the VR experience.

C162.name: Multicore processor
C162.definition: Multicore processor is a type of processor that significantly increases computational capacity. It supports tasks much better than non-multicore or unicore processors.

C163.name: Visual display
C163.definition: Visual display is a device designed to stimulate the user's visual sense, which is the sense of sight. These displays are used to render the experience in virtual and augmented reality.

C164.name: Head-mounted displays
C164.definition: Head-mounted displays (HMDs) are wearable and mobile pieces of equipment that integrate electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components. HMDs place images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens.

C165.name: World-fixed displays
C165.definition: World-fixed displays are stationary display surfaces that render graphics onto surfaces that do not move with the user's head. These displays range from standard monitors to large screens that completely surround the user.

C166.name: Regular displays
C166.definition: Regular displays are mobile or stationary devices, such as tablets or smartphones. These displays are typically relevant for non-immersive virtual reality and are often used for augmented reality.

C167.name: Haptics
C167.definition: Haptics are outputs that explore the sense of touch perception, and they can be categorized based on various criteria. These outputs are used to provide physical feedback in virtual environments.

C168.name: Passive device
C168.definition: Passive device is a static physical object that is not controlled by the computer, allowing users to feel interaction with virtual objects. These devices match the shape of the virtual objects in the real world.

C169.name: Active device
C169.definition: Active device is a physical object that provides feedback and is controlled by the computer to give a sense of touch when dealing with virtual objects. These devices are used to simulate touch in virtual experiences.

C170.name: Tactile sensation
C170.definition: Tactile sensation is a type of touch obtained through the skin, where the skin itself is activated by the output device. This sensation provides the user with a sense of touch.

C171.name: Proprioceptive force
C171.definition: Proprioceptive force is a type of sensation that activates the user's joints or muscles. This force provides a sense of limb movement and muscular resistance.

C172.name: Motion platform
C172.definition: Motion platform is a hardware device that moves the entire body, resulting in a sense of physical motion and gravity, while conveying orientation, vibration, acceleration, and jerks.

C173.name: Active motion platform
C173.definition: Active motion platform is a type of motion platform that is controlled by computer simulation, meaning the computer controls the platform's movement.

C174.name: Passive motion platform
C174.definition: Passive motion platform is a type of motion platform that is controlled by the user, and therefore has no direct computer control.

C175.name: Treadmill
C175.definition: Treadmill is an output device that provides the sensation of walking or running while the user remains in one place by providing different sorts of input to the feet or legs.

C176.name: Omnidirectional treadmill
C176.definition: Omnidirectional treadmill is a common type of treadmill in virtual reality systems that can be either active, meaning it is computer-controlled, or passive, meaning it is user-controlled.

C177.name: Headsets and glasses
C177.definition: Headsets and glasses are a category of augmented reality devices used to provide AR experiences. Examples of this category include AR HoloLens and Google Glass.

C178.name: Handheld devices
C178.definition: Handheld devices are a category of augmented reality hardware that includes devices such as smartphones and tablets. These devices can be used for various applications like e-commerce and tourism.

C179.name: Projection-based systems
C179.definition: Projection-based systems are augmented reality devices that utilize methods like interactive projectors and AR sandboxes. These systems are used in fields such as industrial design and medical training.

C180.name: Head-up displays
C180.definition: Head-up displays are a type of AR hardware that is typically found in vehicles. These displays can be integrated into gaming experiences, medicine, and sports.

C181.name: Spatial AR
C181.definition: Spatial AR is a type of augmented reality that serves as a prime example of multi-user engagement, allowing multiple users to interact with augmented digital content in a physical space.

C182.name: High-definition hologram
C182.definition: High-definition hologram is the digital content that is integrated with the real-world view. This content is projected onto the user's view, allowing the digital information to appear in the physical environment.

C183.name: Depth sensor
C183.definition: Depth sensor is a component used in spatial AR systems to achieve seamless mixing of digital and physical elements. It helps the system understand the physical environment's geometry and lighting conditions.

C184.name: Smart glasses
C184.definition: Smart glasses are a category of AR devices that are typically lighter and resemble standard eyeglasses. They are used for AR application deployment but are less immersive than Head-Mounted Displays.

C185.name: 3D hologram
C185.definition: A 3D hologram is a complex visual output provided by AR headsets. This contrasts with the simpler digital content overlays found in smart glasses.

C186.name: See-through display
C186.definition: A see-through display is a component, such as the glass part of a device, that allows the user to view the real world while receiving AR content. It is one of the many components found in advanced AR glasses.

C187.name: Marker-based AR
C187.definition: Marker-based AR is a type of augmented reality where specific markers are placed in the real world. The system recognizes these markers using image recognition to augment specific content.

C188.name: Augmented content
C188.definition: Augmented content is virtual information that is overlaid onto the live streaming of the real world environment. This overlaying of virtual information happens on top of the screen.

C189.name: Spatial AR device
C189.definition: Spatial AR device is a type of augmented reality where digital content is overlaid onto specific physical objects, rather than being overlaid onto the user's view of the real world. The defining feature is that the display element is independent of the user.

C190.name: Virtual object
C190.definition: Virtual object is a digital element that is added to the physical environment, appearing to coexist within the same space as the real objects. The fundamental principle of spatial AR is augmenting the physical environment by adding these virtual objects.

C191.name: Room-scale AR
C191.definition: Room-scale AR is a specific type of augmented reality where devices typically use projectors to display graphical information directly onto physical objects. This contrasts with other AR types where content is overlaid on the user's view.

C192.name: Projection-based AR system
C192.definition: Projection-based AR system is a method of augmented reality where digital content is displayed onto physical surfaces using projectors. This category is generally similar to spatial AR systems.

C193.name: Interactive display
C193.definition: Interactive display is a surface that is converted into a display by projecting images onto it, allowing users to interact with the projected content.

C194.name: AR contact lens
C194.definition: An AR contact lens is a future wearable device that superimposes digital images or information directly onto the wearer's field of vision via the lens. These lenses are very small and can be placed directly on the eye like a regular contact lens.

C195.name: Headsets
C195.definition: Headsets are an older type of wearable AR hardware that represents an outdated concept in the field.

C196.name: Glasses
C196.definition: Glasses are a modern, state-of-the-art wearable AR device that is rapidly advancing in development.

C197.name: Contact lenses (AR contact lenses)
C197.definition: AR contact lenses are an upcoming, state-of-the-art technology that could become very popular if affordability is achieved.

C198.name: Sensing
C198.definition: Sensing is a term often used interchangeably with tracking, referring to the requirement of tracking in both AR and VR systems.

C199.name: Sense organ tracking
C199.definition: Sense organ tracking involves tracking the user's sense organs, such as eyes and ears, whose degrees of freedom are controlled by the body. This tracking is necessary so that the position and orientation of the organ can be reflected in the virtual world.

C200.name: Other body part tracking
C200.definition: Other body part tracking involves tracking parts of the user's body that are not sense organs, such as hands or facial features. This is required when the user needs to see a representation of their body in the virtual world, such as through avatars.

C201.name: Environment tracking
C201.definition: Environment tracking involves tracking physical objects in the real world that surround the user. This is crucial in augmented reality (AR) to properly register digital content in 3D, and in virtual reality (VR) to prevent physical harm.

C202.name: Live capture
C202.definition: Live capture is a method used to bring a large part of the physical world into the virtual world. This allows the virtual world to be augmented with a real-world representation.

C203.name: Outside-in tracking
C203.definition: Outside-in tracking is a method where the trackers or sensors are part of the environment, rather than being part of the devices the user is wearing or using.

C204.name: Inside-out tracking
C204.definition: Inside-out tracking is a method where the tracker carries the sensors that are integrated into the devices the user is wearing or using.

C205.name: Calibration
C205.definition: Calibration is the phase where the tracker is oriented as close to the real world as possible.

C206.name: Registration
C206.definition: Registration is the step used to estimate or determine the starting position and orientation of the sensor. Knowing this initial location is necessary before tracking movement can begin.

C207.name: Integration
C207.definition: Integration is the step where sensory measurements are aggregated at specific, discrete points in time. This process combines data from multiple sensors to effectively track the target object or environment.

C208.name: Drift correction
C208.definition: Drift correction is the phase that compensates for the mismatch between the estimated position and orientation and the actual values. This process aims to reduce the error in the tracking estimation.

C209.name: Inside-out
C209.definition: Inside-out refers to a tracker where all the necessary sensors are placed directly onto the device that the user is utilizing.

C210.name: Outside-in
C210.definition: Outside-in refers to a tracker that utilizes sensors placed within the surrounding environment, rather than placing them on the user's device.

C211.name: Gyroscope
C211.definition: Gyroscope is a sensor that captures the angular velocity of movement.

C212.name: Accelerometer
C212.definition: Accelerometer is a sensor that captures the linear acceleration along the three axes: x, y, and z.

C213.name: Magnetometer
C213.definition: Magnetometer is a sensor that captures the magnetic field strength along the three axes.

C214.name: Measurement error
C214.definition: Measurement error is the difference between the measured value from a sensor and the actual, ideal value. This difference occurs because sensors are imperfect devices.

C215.name: Sum of squared errors
C215.definition: Sum of squared errors is a method used to compare data from two sensor types by computing the difference between corresponding values, squaring that difference, and then summing all the resulting squared values across all samples.

C216.name: Linear least squares
C216.definition: Linear least squares is a classical regression problem used to optimize a function by minimizing the square term of the difference between the predicted and actual values.

C217.name: Fiducial marker
C217.definition: Fiducial marker is a tag or reflector used to significantly aid in the registration process. These markers help the tracking system achieve accurate alignment.

C218.name: Initial orientation
C218.definition: Initial orientation is the direction the headset is facing when the tracking system is first turned on. This setting establishes the forward direction for the initial alignment.

C219.name: Angular velocity sample
C219.definition: Angular velocity sample is the sample of angular velocity obtained from the gyroscopic sensor at a specific instant. This sample indicates the rotation or change in orientation.

C220.name: Gain parameter
C220.definition: Gain parameter is a normalized value between 0 and 1 used in drift correction. This parameter is applied to combine the separately estimated orientation at a specific time instant.

C221.name: Orientation
C221.definition: Orientation is the estimated direction of a tracked body part or object at any arbitrary instant of time. This orientation is determined by summing the sensory values, starting from the initial orientation estimated during the registration phase.

C222.name: Electromechanical tracker
C222.definition: Electromechanical tracker consists of a serial or parallel kinematic structure composed of links that are interconnected using joints and equipped with sensors. These trackers are used to capture movement data in virtual and augmented reality environments.

C223.name: World-fixed electromechanical tracker
C223.definition: World-fixed electromechanical tracker is a type of electromechanical tracker that is stationary and fixed in a specific environment. This setup typically includes a display, mechanical pivoting, and tracking sensors attached to the entire structure.

C224.name: Wearable tracker
C224.definition: Wearable tracker is a type of electromechanical tracker that is designed to be worn directly on the body of the user. These trackers capture real human movements which are then translated into virtual world movements.

C225.name: Avatar
C225.definition: Avatar is an animated representation of a real human being that is created using wearable trackers. The movements of the human wearing the tracker are tracked and translated to the avatar's movement in the virtual world.

C226.name: Electromagnetic tracker
C226.definition: Electromagnetic tracker is a non-contact position measurement device that tracks movement by using a magnetic field generated by a stationary transmitter. This field determines the real-time position of a moving receiver element.

C227.name: Acoustic tracking
C227.definition: Acoustic tracking is a method of tracking that utilizes ultrasonic signals to determine the real-time position of a moving object. This technique is also referred to as ultrasonic tracking.

C228.name: Line of sight
C228.definition: Line of sight is a requirement for acoustic tracking, meaning the transmitter and receiver must be within the visual range of each other. There must not be any obstacle positioned between the two devices.

C229.name: Vision-based tracker
C229.definition: Vision-based tracker is a type of tracker that determines poses, such as position and orientation, using optical sensors or cameras. These trackers are currently very prevalent in the field.

C230.name: Optical sensor
C230.definition: Optical sensor is a device that determines poses by using optical means, such as cameras. These sensors are categorized into infrared, visible light, and 3D structure types.

C231.name: Infrared tracking
C231.definition: Infrared tracking is a vision-based technique that utilizes targets which either emit or reflect infrared light. This method is robust to adverse illumination effects, such as poor ambient lighting or harsh shadows.

C232.name: Outside looking in
C232.definition: Outside looking in is a tracking method where targets are attached to the object being tracked, but the cameras are placed externally in the environment. The cameras detect the targets and use this information to determine the object's pose and position.

C233.name: Visible light tracking
C233.definition: Visible light tracking is a method that utilizes visible light sensors or optical cameras to perform tracking. These sensors are commonly found in consumer-grade electronic devices and wearable devices.

C234.name: Fiducial tracking
C234.definition: Fiducial tracking is a method that uses artificial landmarks added to the environment to aid in registration and tracking. These artificial landmarks allow the system to track specific objects or areas within the environment.

C235.name: Natural feature tracking
C235.definition: Natural feature tracking registers camera pose in real time using features that are already present in the natural environment. This process requires advanced image processing algorithms to detect unique features such as points, corners, and line intersections.

C236.name: Model-based tracking
C236.definition: Model-based tracking is a visible light sensing category that involves techniques for mapping and localization within a real environment. This technique is often used to simultaneously create and update a map while tracking positions.

C237.name: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping
C237.definition: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is a technique that simultaneously creates and updates a map of the real environment while localizing positions within it. This technique was originally developed for robot navigation and has since been adapted for augmented reality.

C238.name: 3D structure tracking
C238.definition: 3D structure tracking is a technique that uses sensors to obtain information about the three-dimensional positions of points within a scene. This technique involves creating 3D models of the environment and using them for tracking.

C239.name: 3D model
C239.definition: A 3D model is a digital representation created from real objects or environments. These models are used for tracking the pose of devices or for augmenting the real-world view.

C240.name: 3D structure sensing
C240.definition: 3D structure sensing is the process of creating 3D models of the structures present in an environment. This process is used specifically for the augmentation of the real-world view.

C241.name: Inertial tracker
C241.definition: Inertial tracker is a self-contained sensor that measures changes in an object's orientation, translation velocity, or acceleration. These trackers are typically based on microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) and have no range limitations.

C242.name: Microelectromechanical systems
C242.definition: Microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) are a type of technology typically used in inertial trackers. This technology allows the sensors to be integrated into the user's device without any range limitations.

C243.name: Real Time Kinematic technology
C243.definition: Real Time Kinematic technology (RTK) is an enhancement to basic GPS that uses GPS signal carrier waves for measurement. This technology provides greater accuracy compared to a basic GPS system.

C244.name: Gyroscope
C244.definition: Gyroscope is one of the primary inertial sensors, alongside the accelerometer and magnetometer. These sensors are used to design hybrid software-level sensors that can be part of a device.

C245.name: Motion capture
C245.definition: Motion capture is the technique of digitally recording movements of real things, usually humans. This technique can be based on any tracking method.

C246.name: Eye-tracking system
C246.definition: Eye-tracking system is a type of tracker that can be incorporated into other trackers. Such a system typically tracks the gaze point or area of the gaze of the user.

C247.name: Optical tracking
C247.definition: Optical tracking is a method that utilizes a high-resolution camera-based tracking device. This method is used to record movements.

C248.name: Hybrid tracker
C248.definition: A hybrid tracker is a tracking method that utilizes two or more basic tracking systems. This combination of systems is employed to achieve the tracking goal.

C249.name: VR software
C249.definition: VR software is the program that must support key components and user locomotion. This software is essential for building and deploying virtual reality systems.

C250.name: Input device
C250.definition: Input devices are utilized by the user to perform an operation that generates data. This generated data is then sent into the VR system for processing.

C251.name: Output device
C251.definition: Output devices are responsible for generating suitable stimuli. These stimuli are intended to affect the user's sense organs.

C252.name: Rendering
C252.definition: Rendering is the process of creating the stereoscopic view, which serves as the output of the VR experience. This term is used broadly and can refer to stimulation of senses other than the visual sense.

C253.name: Software Development Kit
C253.definition: Software Development Kit (SDK) is a tool utilized for specific headsets that manages low-level operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output.

C254.name: Platform
C254.definition: Platform is a broader term than headset, referring to a specific combination of hardware and operating system.

C255.name: Game engine
C255.definition: Game engine is a type of middleware specifically created or adapted for generating VR experiences, though it was originally developed for building any type of game.

C256.name: Virtual world generator
C256.definition: Virtual world generator is an abstraction of the entire software system that converts input information into output so that the experience appears real to the user. It is responsible for maintaining the internal reality of the virtual environment.

C257.name: Internal reality
C257.definition: Internal reality is the state that the Virtual world generator maintains so that the virtual experience appears real to the user. This maintained reality allows renderers to extract necessary information to calculate outputs for the displays.

C258.name: Input events
C258.definition: Input events are data that arrive from low-level systems, such as a head tracker or game controller, and are arranged in a queue for systematic processing by the software.

C259.name: Virtual world
C259.definition: Virtual world is a scene, which may be completely synthetic or based on a recorded physical world, that is rendered visually for the user. This world comprises the visual display.

C260.name: Triangular mesh
C260.definition: Triangular mesh is a structure created by defining numerous triangles in a 3D space, which is required to create a synthetic scene. This mesh is the fundamental geometric representation of the scene.

C261.name: Computer graphics
C261.definition: Computer graphics addresses computer-generated images that are derived from synthetic models. The software used to build an application must support these computer graphics operations.

C262.name: Texture mapping
C262.definition: Texture mapping is an operation where camera images taken of a real object are mapped onto a synthetic object within the virtual world. This is a common operation in computer graphics.

C263.name: Material properties
C263.definition: Material properties are the physical characteristics of surfaces that indicate how they interact with elements such as light, sound, and forces. These properties must be maintained alongside the geometric mesh.

C264.name: Matched motion
C264.definition: Matched motion is the correspondence between user motions in the real world and the virtual world. This ensures that the virtual environment accurately reflects the user's physical movements.

C265.name: Matched zone
C265.definition: Matched zone is a specific area where the real and virtual worlds perfectly align. Within this zone, the user can move physically in the real world, and that movement is translated to the virtual world.

C266.name: Locomotion
C266.definition: Locomotion is the act of moving oneself within the virtual world when the user's physical motion is not matched in the real world. This allows users to explore virtual environments without making corresponding physical movements.

C267.name: Mismatch of obstacles
C267.definition: Mismatch of obstacles occurs when there is a discrepancy between physical and virtual barriers in the matched zone. This happens when a user can be blocked by a virtual obstacle but not a physical one, or vice versa.

C268.name: User locomotion
C268.definition: User locomotion is a concern regarding how a user moves themselves within the virtual world. Support for user locomotion is important to address potential sickness issues.

C269.name: Avatar
C269.definition: Avatar is the representation of the user in the virtual world. This avatar can perform activities like walking, running, or swimming without the user needing to move physically.

C270.name: Vehicle metaphor
C270.definition: Vehicle metaphor is an alternative way to move in the virtual world. This metaphor allows the user to operate controls to move themselves while remaining seated.

C271.name: Computer graphics operations
C271.definition: Computer graphics operations is the required support for synthetic virtual world generation.

C272.name: Computer vision
C272.definition: Computer vision is a required support for realistic virtual world generation, often used in combination with other techniques.

C273.name: Texture synthesis
C273.definition: Texture synthesis is a method used in realistic virtual world generation that requires support from computer graphics.

C274.name: Physics support
C274.definition: Physics support is a required feature that ensures the virtual world behaves like the real world by governing how objects move and interacting with physical phenomena. This support includes replicating how light, sound, and smell propagate through the environment.

C275.name: Collision detection algorithm
C275.definition: The collision detection algorithm is the support that determines whether two or more bodies are intersecting in the virtual world. It also dictates how those intersecting bodies should behave.

C276.name: Collision response
C276.definition: Collision response is the appropriate action needed after a collision takes place. This response determines how objects should react when they intersect with other objects.

C277.name: Basic laws of mechanics
C277.definition: Basic laws of mechanics are the fundamental rules that should govern how objects move in the virtual world. Support for these laws is considered sufficient for the virtual world to function.

C278.name: Shared virtual world
C278.definition: A shared virtual world is a digital environment that is maintained and hosted by a dedicated system or server. This environment allows multiple users to interact within the same space.

C279.name: Matched zone
C279.definition: A matched zone is a distinct area assigned to each user within the virtual world. These zones may either overlap in the real world or be disjoint and distributed globally.

C280.name: Physics
C280.definition: Physics, in the context of a virtual world, refers to the algorithms that govern how objects behave within the environment. This includes handling movement, detecting collisions, and determining the response to those collisions.

C281.name: Game engine
C281.definition: Game engine is a middleware that sits between the hardware and higher-level application software, abstracting hardware functionalities for developers of Extended Reality (XR) applications.

C282.name: Collaborative VR experience
C282.definition: A Collaborative VR experience is a virtual reality setting that supports multiple users interacting within the same environment. This requires additional support beyond basic physics and rendering, often involving network capabilities.

C283.name: Rendering engine
C283.definition: Rendering engine is a component designed to help generate animated 3D graphics by utilizing various methods.

C284.name: Audio engine
C284.definition: Audio engine consists of algorithms related to loading, modifying, and generating sound through a speaker system.

C285.name: Physics engine
C285.definition: Physics engine is a crucial component responsible for emulating the laws of physics within an application.

C286.name: Rasterization
C286.definition: Rasterization is a rendering technique that is less computationally intensive when compared to the ray tracing method.

C287.name: Native application
C287.definition: Native application is a type of deployment that requires the use of Software Development Kits (SDKs) specifically tailored to the platform and hardware.

C288.name: Head-mounted display
C288.definition: Head-mounted display (HMD) is the most popular type of device used for experiencing virtual reality.

C289.name: Web deployment
C289.definition: Web deployment refers to the method of deploying systems so that they can be accessed and run over the web.

C290.name: Augmented reality software (AR Software)
C290.definition: Augmented reality software is the specific set of tools and programs used for implementing augmented reality. This technology area is being discussed alongside virtual reality.

C291.name: Low-level software libraries
C291.definition: Low-level software libraries are tools that require considerable skill from the developer. Developers must possess skill in both understanding the library functions and in coding to call those functions.

C292.name: Standalone AR authoring tools
C292.definition: Standalone AR authoring tools are types of software designed for novice users or developers. These tools assume that the user does not require any programming skill to operate them.

C293.name: Framework
C293.definition: Framework is a combination of multiple libraries created to facilitate Augmented Reality system development. This combination allows developers to overcome the limitations of single, low-level toolkits.

C294.name: Low-level library
C294.definition: Low-level libraries provide access to the core tracking and display functionality necessary to build an Augmented Reality application. These libraries require strong programming ability from the developer.

C295.name: Scene graph
C295.definition: Scene graph represents computer graphic scenes as a node-based graph. This structure allows the entire scene to be represented as a tree, enabling selective manipulation and realistic effects.

C296.name: 3D registration
C296.definition: 3D registration is the process of creating and rendering a three-dimensional object at a specific position in the real world. This operation is necessary after the system has recognized a marker or feature.

C297.name: Rapid prototyping and development tools
C297.definition: Rapid prototyping and development tools are software used to quickly visualize or create prototypes of an idea before committing to major coding efforts. These tools allow users to test ideas simply rather than going through the entire coding exercise.

C298.name: Authoring tool
C298.definition: An authoring tool is a popular software used for creating prototypes that include multimedia content for web and desktop platforms. These tools allow the creation of a variety of desktop and mobile experiences.

C299.name: AR toolkit
C299.definition: An AR toolkit is a version of an Augmented Reality (AR) toolkit that has been ported over to a specific platform, such as Flash. This toolkit enables users to have an AR experience directly from within their web browser.

C300.name: 3D registering
C300.definition: 3D registering is the process of loading and overlaying virtual content onto a tracked image. This allows the virtual content to be correctly placed in the real-world view.

C301.name: Rapid prototyping tools
C301.definition: Rapid prototyping tools are specialized tools used to quickly create an initial version of an Augmented Reality application, allowing developers to continue work on various categories of AR software.

C302.name: Open Frameworks
C302.definition: Open Frameworks is an open-source C++ middleware library that functions as a combination of multiple libraries, designed to support interactive experiences on both desktop and mobile platforms.

C303.name: Non-web-based authoring tools
C303.definition: Non-web-based authoring tools are specialized tools designed to create Augmented Reality experiences that run natively on mobile and desktop platforms.

C304.name: Wikitude
C304.definition: Wikitude is an example of a prototyping tool that functions as an AR browser application, typically used for mobile experiences.

C305.name: Client device
C305.definition: A client device, in the context of AR architecture, is primarily treated as a rendering device or a client that connects back to a backend server for content provision and computation.

C306.name: Low-level libraries and frameworks
C306.definition: Low-level libraries and frameworks are tools that require the highest level of programming skill when dealing with AR software. These are situated at one extreme of the spectrum of required programming ability.

C307.name: Plugin
C307.definition: Plugins require a basic authoring tool to function, and AR support is provided through this add-on software. Plugins do not come as a complete package but rely on an existing basic software to provide AR functionality.

C308.name: Content authoring tool
C308.definition: A content authoring tool is a software application that allows a user to create interactive 2D or 3D content. This tool is the base software that plugins are added to.

C309.name: Software library
C309.definition: A software library is a collection of code that requires programming skills to understand and utilize. Users must learn or master these libraries to use them effectively.

C310.name: Interactive 3D graphics authoring tool
C310.definition: Interactive 3D graphics authoring tools are programs used to create interactive 3D applications, such as Unity or Vizard. Most of these tools include plugins specifically for AR visualization.

C311.name: Plugin-based approach
C311.definition: Plugin-based tools provide an easy and quick method for developing AR applications. However, this approach restricts the developer's flexibility in deciding on interaction methods or interface look and feel.

C312.name: Marker-based tracking
C312.definition: Marker-based tracking is a type of computer vision-based tracking that provides AR visualization support. This method is one of the options available for AR visualization.

C313.name: Mobile AR application
C313.definition: Mobile AR applications are AR programs that function on both iOS and Android platforms. These applications can be created using plugins like Vuforia that work with Unity 3D.

C314.name: Low-level software development tool
C314.definition: Low-level software development tools are used to build a custom system from scratch rather than depending on a third-party tool. This method is employed to resolve the issues and cons associated with high-level authoring tools.

C315.name: Standalone authoring tool
C315.definition: Standalone authoring tools are software that require the least amount of programming skill when working with AR software. These tools represent the opposite extreme of the programming skill requirement spectrum.

C316.name: Scene construction
C316.definition: Scene construction is a function supported by authoring tools that allows developers to build the environment or setting for the AR experience. This function is one of the typical sets of capabilities provided by these tools.

C317.name: Interactive behavior
C317.definition: Interactive behavior is a function that allows developers to add dynamic responses and actions to the elements within the AR scene. This capability can range from limited support to extensive support depending on the software package.

C318.name: Graphical user interface
C318.definition: Graphical user interface (GUI) is a visual interface, often drag-and-drop type, that developers use to create an application or experience. This interface allows users to create an experience without requiring coding.

C319.name: Human factors
C319.definition: Human factors refers to the aspects of the user experience that affect how people interact with Extended reality systems. These factors are relevant during the building and deployment of both Augmented reality and Virtual reality experiences.

C320.name: Plugins to existing systems
C320.definition: Plugins to existing systems are a category of tools that allow for integration into pre-existing systems. This category is one of the types of tools available for AR software development.

C321.name: Interactive systems
C321.definition: Interactive systems are a broad class of systems that includes extended reality, and understanding them requires knowing their core concerns. These systems are the foundational category to which extended reality systems belong.

C322.name: Ubiquitous computing
C322.definition: Ubiquitous computing is a state where users can access multiple connected computers that communicate with each other, allowing the user to operate them without separate intervention.

C323.name: Layman user
C323.definition: Layman user is a person who uses a system without being a technology expert, focusing only on using the system rather than understanding its internal workings.

C324.name: Lay person
C324.definition: A lay person is an end user who is not necessarily an expert in the technology behind the system. Designers of interactive systems should cater to these users without forcing them to learn complex technical details.

C325.name: Technical jargon
C325.definition: Technical jargon refers to specialized language or terms, such as 'security accounts manager,' that are unlikely to be understood by laypersons. Using such terms in user interfaces can confuse and potentially frustrate the user.

C326.name: User-centric approach
C326.definition: User-centric approach is a process for designing computer systems by considering the characteristics, needs, and expectations of the users. This method ensures that the system is designed to meet the specific requirements of the people who will use it.

C327.name: System state
C327.definition: System state is the exact condition of the system as perceived by the user, focusing on what is happening from the user's point of view rather than technical details. This perception helps the user understand the current status of the system.

C328.name: Goal state
C328.definition: Goal state is the final condition a user reaches after transitioning through various states to successfully complete a desired task or work. Users transition between states until they achieve this ultimate goal.

C329.name: Layouts
C329.definition: Layouts are the methods by which interface elements are organized on a screen or interface. These arrangements must meet the expectations of the user.

C330.name: User characteristics
C330.definition: User characteristics refers to the specific traits and knowledge of the user that must be understood during system design. Knowledge of these characteristics is essential for building an appropriate system.

C331.name: Interface
C331.definition: Interface is the mechanism provided to the user that allows them to input information, view outcomes, and act based on those outcomes. The required interface depends heavily on the user's technical expertise.

C332.name: Querying language
C332.definition: Querying language is a technical skill or language used by advanced users to retrieve information from a database. This language is typically known by technical experts, unlike general users.

C333.name: Interactive system
C333.definition: Interactive systems are a type of system characterized by a basic idea that differentiates it from other systems. These systems require specific design concerns to ensure effective user engagement.

C334.name: Novice
C334.definition: Novice is the first class of users who are typically using a system for the first time and are unlikely to have prior knowledge of how the system works.

C335.name: Intermittent
C335.definition: Intermittent is the second class of users who utilize a system occasionally, having used it for a limited duration or number of times.

C336.name: Expert
C336.definition: Expert is the third class of users who have used a system regularly over a long period of time, allowing them to understand all aspects and use it very efficiently.

C337.name: User categorization
